name: Pons
func: The bulging middle part of the brainstem. It relays signals from the cortex to the cerebellum, helps control breathing rhythm and sleep, and holds the nuclei for chewing, facial movement, outward eye movement and balance.

levels.kid:
The **pons** is a round bump on the stalk at the bottom of your brain. "Pons" means **bridge**, and that is its job: it is a bridge that carries messages between the big thinking part of your brain and the little balance part at the back.

The pons helps you **breathe** smoothly, even when you are asleep and not thinking about it. It helps you **chew** your food, **smile** and blink, and look to the side.

It also helps you fall asleep and **dream**. When you dream about flying, the pons keeps your body still in bed so you don't actually try to fly!
levels.hs:
The **pons** is the middle section of the **brainstem**, between the **midbrain** above and the **medulla oblongata** below. It sits in front of the **cerebellum**, and the **fourth ventricle** lies between them. Its front surface is a big rounded bulge resting against the **clivus** of the skull, with the **basilar artery** running up the midline groove.

The pons has two parts:
- The **basilar pons** (front): masses of **pontine nuclei** that pass messages from the cerebral cortex across the midline to the opposite cerebellum through the thick **middle cerebellar peduncles**. This is how your cortex "tells" the cerebellum what movement it plans.
- The **tegmentum** (back): cranial nerve nuclei and pathways.

Four cranial nerves are tied to the pons: the **trigeminal (V)** for facial sensation and chewing, the **abducens (VI)** for turning the eye outward, the **facial (VII)** for facial expression and taste, and the **vestibulocochlear (VIII)** for hearing and balance, which enters at the junction with the medulla.

Pontine centers also smooth out breathing rhythm and help generate **REM sleep**.
levels.college:
The **basilar pons** contains descending **corticospinal** and **corticobulbar** fibers broken into bundles by the pontine nuclei, plus **corticopontine** fibers that synapse there. **Pontocerebellar** fibers cross the midline and form the **middle cerebellar peduncle**, the largest cerebellar input.

In the dorsal tegmentum, the **abducens nucleus** lies under the **facial colliculus** in the floor of the fourth ventricle. The bump is made by **facial nerve fibers looping around the abducens nucleus** (the internal genu). The **medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)** links the abducens nucleus to the opposite oculomotor nucleus for conjugate horizontal gaze. The **paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF)** is the horizontal gaze center.

The **trigeminal nuclei** span the brainstem: the **principal sensory nucleus** (touch) and **motor nucleus** (chewing muscles) are in the mid-pons; the **mesencephalic nucleus** extends up into the midbrain; the **spinal nucleus** runs down into the cervical cord. The **vestibular** and **cochlear nuclei** lie at the pontomedullary junction, and the **superior olivary complex** compares sound timing between the ears.

The **pneumotaxic** (pontine respiratory group, in the parabrachial area) and **apneustic** centers modulate the medullary rhythm generator. The **locus coeruleus**, the main noradrenaline source of the brain, sits in the rostral pons.

Arterial supply comes from **paramedian** and **circumferential** branches of the basilar artery, plus the **AICA** and **SCA**.
levels.phd:
Several pontine circuits are under active study. The **locus coeruleus (LC)** contains roughly tens of thousands of neurons per side yet sends noradrenergic axons to nearly the whole neuraxis. Its tonic versus phasic firing modes are linked to arousal and to the **adaptive gain** theory of attention (Aston-Jones and Cohen). LC neurons are among the earliest sites of tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease (Braak stage 0–I).

**REM sleep** depends on pontine networks: glutamatergic neurons of the **sublaterodorsal nucleus** (subcoeruleus) project to the ventromedial medulla and spinal interneurons, which inhibit motor neurons and produce **REM atonia**. Their loss lets people act out dreams (**REM sleep behavior disorder**), a strong prodromal marker of alpha-synucleinopathies. Cholinergic neurons of the **pedunculopontine** and **laterodorsal tegmental nuclei** promote REM and wakefulness. **PGO waves** (ponto-geniculo-occipital) arise in the pons during REM.

The **pontine nuclei** relay cortical information as **mossy fibers** to cerebellar granule cells, forming the cortico-ponto-cerebellar loop. The **Kölliker–Fuse** and **parabrachial nuclei** shape the transition from inspiration to expiration (inspiratory off-switch); lesions combined with vagotomy cause **apneusis**.

The **superior olive** computes sound localization: the **medial superior olive** detects interaural time differences using coincidence-detector neurons (a modified Jeffress model with precisely timed glycinergic inhibition), and the **lateral superior olive** compares interaural level differences, receiving inhibition through the **medial nucleus of the trapezoid body** via the giant **calyx of Held** synapse, a model for studying transmitter release.
levels.expert:
Pontine lesions are some of the most dramatic in neurology.

- **Locked-in syndrome**: a bilateral ventral pontine infarct (often **basilar artery occlusion**) leaves the patient awake but quadriplegic and unable to speak; vertical eye movements and blinking are spared because the midbrain is intact. It is a reason never to assume an unresponsive patient is unaware.
- **Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)**: an **MLF** lesion causes failure of adduction of the eye on the lesion side with nystagmus of the abducting eye; convergence is preserved. Bilateral INO in a young adult suggests **multiple sclerosis**.
- **One-and-a-half syndrome**: PPRF or abducens nucleus plus MLF lesion; the only horizontal movement left is abduction of one eye.
- **Millard–Gubler syndrome**: ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis.
- **Pinpoint pupils** with coma suggest a **pontine hemorrhage** (often hypertensive), from loss of sympathetic pathways.

**Osmotic demyelination syndrome** (central pontine myelinolysis) follows overly rapid correction of low sodium; MRI shows a trident-shaped T2 lesion in the central pons. **Diffuse midline glioma** (H3 K27-altered, formerly DIPG) is a devastating pediatric pontine tumor; diagnosis is often made on MRI, it is not resectable, and radiotherapy is the mainstay.

The **cerebellopontine angle** is surgically crucial: **vestibular schwannomas** arise there, causing one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus; options include observation, stereotactic radiosurgery, or microsurgery with facial nerve monitoring. Pontine **cavernous malformations** may be resected through "safe entry zones" in the floor of the fourth ventricle.

keyPoints: Middle brainstem segment, in front of the cerebellum and fourth ventricle
Pontine nuclei → middle cerebellar peduncle: cortex-to-cerebellum relay
Cranial nerves V, VI, VII (and VIII at the pontomedullary junction)
Breathing modulation, REM sleep and the locus coeruleus
Basilar occlusion → locked-in syndrome; MLF lesion → INO

test.q: Which cerebellar peduncle is formed by fibers from the pontine nuclei?
test.explain: The middle cerebellar peduncle carries crossed pontocerebellar fibers, the largest cerebellar input.

test.q: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus causes internuclear ______.
test.explain: INO: the eye on the lesion side cannot adduct on lateral gaze, while convergence is spared.

test.q: A patient who is awake, can blink and look up and down but cannot move limbs or speak most likely has:
test.explain: A ventral pontine infarct destroys corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts but spares consciousness and vertical gaze.

test.q: The bump in the floor of the fourth ventricle called the facial colliculus overlies which nucleus?
test.explain: Facial nerve fibers loop over the abducens nucleus, raising the facial colliculus.

test.q: The main noradrenaline-producing nucleus of the brain, in the rostral pons, is the locus ______.
test.explain: The locus coeruleus projects noradrenaline across the brain and drives arousal and attention.
